title: Kepler
subtitle: The telescope that counted planets
tagline: A bedtime story from deep space

pages.title: Kepler
pages.narration: Sleeping Beauties presents... Kepler. The telescope that counted planets. A bedtime story from deep space.

pages.title: Following the Earth
text: Far away in space, a telescope is drifting along behind the Earth, like a little duckling following its mother around the Sun.
It is tall and round, with a slanted hood on top and a solar panel on its back. Every year, it falls a little farther behind.
Its name is Kepler. It is asleep now.
But for nine years, Kepler stared at the stars without blinking. And it discovered that the night sky is full of planets, more planets than there are stars.
pages.fact: Kepler was named after Johannes Kepler, an astronomer who, about four hundred years ago, worked out how planets move around the Sun.

pages.title: Are There Other Earths?
text: For thousands of years, people have looked up at the stars and wondered: do other stars have planets, like our Sun does? Could some of them be like the Earth?
When Kepler's story began, astronomers had found only a few hundred planets around other stars, and most of them were giants, much bigger than Jupiter.
Small, rocky planets like ours are very hard to see. They are tiny, and they are hidden in the glare of their bright stars.
So scientists asked a big question: are planets like Earth rare, or are they everywhere? To find out, they built Kepler.
pages.fact: Planets that circle stars other than our Sun are called exoplanets.

pages.title: The Biggest Camera in Space
text: Kepler launched on the sixth of March, two thousand and nine.
It was a telescope with a big curved mirror, almost as wide as a grown-up is tall, and at the back, a giant camera. At that time, it was the biggest camera ever sent into space.
Kepler did not circle the Earth. It went around the Sun, following along behind our planet, where it was quiet and still, far from Earth's glow.
Then it turned towards a patch of sky near a group of stars called Cygnus, the Swan, and opened its eye.
pages.fact: Kepler's mirror was 1.4 metres wide, one of the biggest mirrors beyond Earth's orbit at the time.

pages.title: The Tiny Blink
text: Kepler could not see the planets themselves. So how did it find them?
It watched about one hundred and fifty thousand stars, all at once, and measured how bright each one was, over and over again, very, very carefully.
When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a tiny bit of the star's light. The star dims, just a little, like when a moth flies in front of a faraway streetlight. Then it brightens again.
If the same tiny blink came back again and again, regularly, like a clock, that meant a planet was going round and round its star. Kepler had found a new world!
pages.fact: This way of finding planets is called the transit method. A transit is when one thing passes in front of another.

pages.title: Planets Everywhere
text: Within its first six weeks, Kepler found five new planets. And then it found more, and more, and more.

Some planets were bigger than Jupiter. Some were rocky, like the Earth. Some circled two suns at once, like a planet in a space story. Some stars had six, seven, even eight planets, all packed close together.
And some small planets were just the right distance from their stars, not too hot and not too cold, where water could stay liquid on the ground.
The most common kind of planet Kepler found does not even exist in our Solar System: bigger than the Earth, but smaller than Neptune.
pages.fact: Kepler's data showed that many stars in the night sky probably have small, rocky planets where water could be liquid.

pages.title: Two Broken Wheels
text: To stare at the stars without wobbling, Kepler used spinning wheels inside it, a bit like the spinning top that keeps a toy steady.
It needed three working wheels to keep perfectly still. But in two thousand and thirteen, a second wheel broke. Now there were only two.
Kepler began to drift. The gentle push of sunlight kept nudging it, and it could not hold its gaze. Its first mission was over.
Was this the end? The team on Earth thought, and thought. And then they had a very clever idea.
pages.fact: Even sunlight pushes on a spacecraft, very gently. Scientists call it solar pressure.

pages.title: Balancing on Sunlight
text: The team turned Kepler so that the sunlight pushed on it evenly, from just the right direction. Like a kayak pointed straight into a river's current, it could stay steady.
Balanced on sunlight, Kepler could hunt for planets again! They called the new mission K2.
Now it could not stare at one patch of sky forever. So every three months or so, it turned to look at a new patch, in what the team called a campaign.
The team hoped to have fuel for about ten campaigns. Kepler managed nineteen!
pages.fact: In K2, Kepler also watched exploding stars, faraway galaxies, and comets and asteroids in our own Solar System.

pages.title: Goodnight, Kepler
text: In two thousand and eighteen, Kepler's fuel ran out at last. On the fifteenth of November, its team sent it a final goodnight message, and switched it off.
That was the very same date that the astronomer Johannes Kepler had died, three hundred and eighty-eight years before.
The telescope Kepler found more than two thousand six hundred planets. It showed us that our galaxy is full of worlds, billions of them, waiting to be explored.
Now it drifts quietly behind the Earth, around and around the Sun. Goodnight, Kepler. Thank you for counting the planets. Look up tonight: so many of those stars have worlds of their own.
pages.fact: A newer telescope called TESS now continues Kepler's work, searching for planets around the brightest stars near us.
